name: Time-Saving Bias
description: People misjudge how much time a speed increase will actually save. We intuitively undervalue moving from slow to moderately faster speeds and overvalue squeezing a little extra speed out of an already fast process.
design_relevance_note: Useful for ETA design, productivity claims, performance dashboards, premium-speed upsells, and optimization roadmaps: teams and users can badly misread which latency improvements meaningfully change total time saved.
prevalence_note: Established in transport and risk-judgment research and occasionally very relevant to digital-performance thinking, but not a mainstream named UX law outside time/latency-sensitive product work.

findings.description: A driving-simulator study found the time-saving bias persists even under active driving with real perceptual feedback, not just in hypothetical scenario judgments -- participants systematically misjudged the speed needed to save a fixed amount of travel time, and this misjudgment affected their actual speed choices. Independently replicates and extends Peer's original hypothetical-scenario finding into a perceptually and behaviorally grounded driving context, by a fully independent research team -- closes this topic's single-study-risk gap with a methodologically distinct demonstration (active behavior, not just judgment surveys).
findings.source_title: The time-saving bias: Judgements, cognition and perception

findings.description: Drivers systematically misestimated time saved by speed increases: they underestimated the savings from moving from slower to moderately faster speeds and overestimated the savings from pushing already-high speeds even higher. These distorted intuitions predicted preferred speeding choices, demonstrating a time-saving bias in intuitive speed/time judgment.
findings.source_title: Speeding and the time-saving bias: How drivers’ estimations of time saved in higher speed affects their choice of speed
